cells.tense: You're under a real load and you're carrying it without going stiff.
cells.ask: Show one person a routine you keep to, and don't explain why it matters. Let them watch what you do with the weight this week.
cells.core: Not the loud push through, not the collapse in a heap — just bearing it, shape intact, still in the room with people while you do it. That steadiness came from repetition, from small work done again and again, and it doesn't flare, so it mostly goes unseen. What you want next isn't more grit. It's someone beside you who doesn't require you to put the weight down first — a connection that doesn't blur into the load. Let one person close enough to watch what you keep doing. It gets easier to keep at it when there's a face in the room. No condition on what comes back.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it and stay yourself while you do.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be borne under weight without going hard
cells.place: in the small repeated work that turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You're bracing for weight that hasn't arrived and may not be yours to hold.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding that no one gave you, set it down for a day, and let it wait or let someone else take it.
cells.core: You're gripping. Not in the practice itself — in every future version of pressure, already rehearsed, already held. The strength you built for the real load got pointed at loads that haven't shown up, and somewhere in the bracing it turned rigid. A plain sense of what's actually yours to carry today, and what isn't, has gone quiet. Fairness is the missing piece: a clean line between the weight on you and the weight you volunteered for. Pick one thing you're holding that nobody handed you and put it down. See what the day gives back when you do. The grip did a job once; this isn't failure, it's letting the load match what's really there.

cells.tense: You came to a door where holding anything felt too dangerous, and you walked away from it.
cells.ask: Finish one small thing this week and let it be done — then leave the space open instead of filling it with the next thing.
cells.core: Going well, this looks like staying under something without hardening: the small repeated work keeps a light on by attention, not by flash. Instead, the practice went quiet. What used to turn intention into skill doesn't run, and more effort pushed in won't help. The answer here isn't bracing harder. Let one thing end, let it be done, and then release it without rushing toward what's next. Letting go is the way through here, not giving up. When the finished thing is allowed to be finished, a little room opens. That space is where the small light starts again, quietly, on its own time.
cells.sheetLine: Standing under weight feels like the start of that, so you don't.

cells.tense: You already hold more than you credit yourself for, and you call it just getting through days.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did because of what you've built in this practice, and say it plainly as yours to do.
cells.core: Something real got built here, and you describe it as though it were nothing — as if you fell into it, or it just happens. Staying under a load without going hard came from something you kept doing. But you've been handing the credit to circumstance, to being wired this way. The shine you notice in people doing what looks like real cultivation is already lit in you. You just haven't claimed it, which means you can't see how far it reaches or where it's leading. There's a direction you'd genuinely want if you admitted you could hold it. Claim one thing, plainly. It belongs to the one who made it.
